summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) solve multi-step, real-world measurement problems that require unit conversion plus calculation or comparison — e.g. scaling a 0.75 kg recipe across 3 batches, or deciding whether 2.5 litres or 2450 ml is more. The new demand beyond pure conversion is SEQUENCING: deciding when and in which direction to convert, putting quantities into a common unit before comparing or operating, labelling units at every step, and sense-checking the final answer's size and unit against an estimate. Classic failures are comparing raw numbers without converting, dropping or reversing the conversion inside a longer chain, treating a decimal measure as two separate whole numbers, and accepting an unreasonable answer unchecked.
misconceptions: Compares measurements without converting to a common unit ('2450 ml > 2.5 l because 2450 > 2.5').
Drops the conversion step or reverses its direction inside a multi-step chain (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 reported as '2.25 g').
Loses track across steps or never estimates, so an unreasonable answer (2250 kg of flour) passes unnoticed.
Treats a mixed/decimal measure as two separate whole numbers when operating.

activities.title: Recipe scaler: convert, operate, and track the unit
steps: Take the problem 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour — how many grams are needed for 3 batches?' and FIRST write a rough estimate of the expected answer (about 2 to 2.5 kg, i.e. roughly 2000–2500 g).
Plan the steps on a bar model or double number line: decide which quantity needs converting and in which direction (0.75 kg → 750 g), then which operation (×3).
Execute either order — convert then operate (0.75 kg → 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g) or operate then convert (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g) — writing the unit on every line of working.
Compare the final answer to your up-front estimate: check both the size and the unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg or '2.25 g' is not).

Repeat with a different context and step order (e.g. mass, capacity, length, time, money) so the method generalises, remembering that time conversions use 60 (minutes/seconds) or 24 (hours/days) rather than 10, 100 or 1000 (e.g. 1.5 hours = 90 minutes, not 150).
activities.insight: A multi-step measurement answer is only trustworthy when each quantity is converted correctly, the unit is carried through every step, and the final size and unit match a sensible up-front estimate.

activities.title: Which is more? Compare on a common-unit number line
steps: Take two measurements in different units — 2.5 litres and 2450 ml — and notice they cannot be judged directly because '2.5' and '2450' are not in the same unit.
Convert one to match the other (2.5 l → 2500 ml, or 2450 ml → 2.45 l), stating which unit you chose and why.
Place both converted values on a single common-unit number line and read off which is larger (2500 ml clearly overtakes 2450 ml).
State the comparison in words: 'you can only compare like with like,' then explain which original measurement was more.
Try further pairs across mass, capacity and length where the raw digits are misleading (e.g. the amount with the bigger bare number is actually smaller).
activities.insight: Two measurements cannot be compared or combined until they are expressed in the same unit; the bare digits can be misleading, so convert to a common unit first.

activities.title: Order the solution steps
steps: For a multi-step problem (e.g. time, distance and unit conversion combined), lay out the solution stages as cards or lines and put them in the correct order BEFORE computing; note that any time conversion uses 60 or 24, not a power of 10.
Decide explicitly where the conversion belongs in the sequence and which direction it goes, then fill in each conversion and operation.
After solving, justify why that order works: say which quantity ends up larger or which operation must come next and why.
Mark where a 'drop-a-step' error would occur if the conversion were skipped, and show what wrong answer it would produce.
activities.insight: Multi-step problems succeed or fail on the ORDER and completeness of steps; naming where the conversion sits in the chain helps prevent dropping or reversing it.

checkQuestion: Set two problems and watch the working: (1) 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?' (2) 'Which is more — 2.5 litres or 2450 ml? How do you know?' Watch whether they convert to a common unit before comparing, whether the conversion step survives the multi-step calculation, and whether they sense-check the size and unit of the answer.
checkAnswer: (1) 0.75 kg = 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g (or 0.75×3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g). (2) 2.5 l = 2500 ml, which is more than 2450 ml. Converts to a common unit, sequences convert-and-operate correctly, and reports a sensible unit.
